Candida Yates  

British object relations, psycho-cultural studies, process, popular culture

This editorial provides a context for this special issue of the journal and outlines its origins in the UK Arts and Humanities Research Council-funded Media and the Inner World research network. In the article, the network directors discuss the significance of British object relations psychoanalytic ideas for shaping new approaches to popular culture. Arguing that the articles constituting this edition contribute toward the formation of a distinctive ‘psycho-cultural’ approach to the application of psychoanalytic theory, the editors outline the main ideas underpinning each contributed article. Maintaining dialogue between the spheres of clinical practice and academic application is paramount here, highlighting the importance of process and demonstrating the specific value of this particular field of theory.

[[RunningHead]]

Lacanian ethics and the assumption of subjectivity

Maria Brock

Maria Brock

UK

Maria Brock  

Calum Neill Basingstoke, Palgrave Macmillan, 2011, 272pp., £55.00/$34.65, ISBN: 978-0230294097

Lacanian Ethics and the Assumption of Subjectivity is the result of the author's longstanding engagement with Lacanian thought. The book aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the French psychoanalyst's ideas on subjectivity and ethics to academics and students at the postgraduate level. It represents a useful starting point for an exploration of the central Lacanian notion of the split subject, alongside such related ideas as fantasy, desire and the drive. In conjunction with Lacan, the author also examines ideas by philosophers such as Levinas, Derrida and, inevitably, Slavoj Žižek.

After a brief excursion into the history of ethics from Plato to Kant, Neill introduces his central question: can Lacan's ideas provide an answer to the question of what exactly can be considered ethical in the age of post-enlightenment? This question is ambitious enough to have occupied such thinkers as Hannah Arendt, Emmanuel Levinas and Paul Ricoeur, and the reader is thus reminded that with this type of book there is always a danger that it may simply become a lengthy exposition of why, in the absence of any universally valid norms or subject positions, it is impossible to provide any satisfying answers.

The first part of the book addresses the subject and begins with a Lacanian take on the Cartesian cogito: rather than the subject's coming into being because of having self-knowledge, this subject must be grasped as opaque. It is barred, lacking, while at the same remaining ignorant of this lack. Early on in the book the author makes one of the text's key points, namely, that ‘assuming a subjective position is already an ethical venture’ (p. 11). If we perceive subjectivity as lacking and unaware of this, then the challenge is one of gaining knowledge of oneself and assuming responsibility for the outcome. Many of the author's concerns resonate strongly with the theme of Judith Butler's (2005)Giving an Account of Oneself. She, too, asks, ‘If it is really true that we are, as it were, divided, ungrounded, or incoherent from the start, will it be impossible to ground a notion of personal or social responsibility?’ (p. 19). In fact, one would do well to read Neill's book along with Butler's, as Butler devotes very little space to the Lacanian subject but is equally interested in the meaning of responsibility towards an other.

Manhood in Hollywood from Bush to Bush

James Morrison

James Morrison

USA

James Morrison  

David Greven University of Texas Press, Austin, 2009, 297pp., paper, $20.10 (purchased from publisher's website), ISBN 978-0292725645; cloth, $36.85 (purchased from publisher's website), ISBN 978-0292719873

The final lines of David Greven's Manhood in Hollywood from Bush to Bush reveal much about the book's aspirations:

Flying into the sunlight, Superman [in Bryan Singer's 2006 film Superman Returns] soaks up the rays, revivifying and restoring himself, embodying the Life Drive as he recalls the beautiful, youthful classical God Apollo, whose beauty is lit by the sun. Images like these live beyond the reactionary patterns of conventional Hollywood film and inspire fresh hopes in the ever-desiring viewer. (p. 245)

It comes as something of a surprise at this late point that Greven finds conventional Hollywood films on the whole “reactionary,” because each of the films he treats in detail emerges as at least ambiguous, if not positively advanced ideologically. These include Casualties of War, Silence of the Lambs, Fight Club, The Passion of the Christ, and Brokeback Mountain – not everyone's idea of the most progressive fare American movies had to offer from 1988 to 2006. Less surprising is that the image in question – from a minor film that Greven declares “flawed but glorious” – is said to “inspire fresh hopes for the ever-desiring viewer.” Greven's book recounts how, in the field of film studies, masochism became a dominant paradigm for envisioning radical possibilities of film texts and spectatorship. Arguing that masochism has been turned to the uses of patriarchy, Greven prefers the model of narcissism, and he makes the case for this counternarrative in a series of imaginative readings of key theoretical texts and corresponding films. And he never gives up. The most obviously retrograde of the films he discusses, The Passion of the Christ, is described as a “beautiful/ugly, hateful/heartrending, offensive/irresistible” (p. 206) and finally “pernicious/affecting” (p. 217) film. Clearly, if even this film lends itself to such wild think-swings, then hope springs eternal.

Hard knocks: Domestic violence and the psychology of storytelling

Abby Stein

Abby Stein

USA

Abby Stein  

Janice Haaken Routledge, London, 2010, 208 pp., $29.99, ISBN-13: 978-0415563420

Janice Haaken, a professor of psychology at Portland (OR) State University, is both a clinician and an advocate for social justice. She has spent a lifetime in the domestic violence trenches and speaks with authority about the movement's goals and modus operandi. She understands that personal life, as well as political life, is a story offered passionately but inaccurately, sometimes half-wittedly, vulnerable to gaps and myriad agenda-driven revisions from within and without. The stories of battered women seem particularly susceptible to these narrative transformations because of their power to incite legal and social change, on one hand, and the deep-seated anxiety they provoke around gendered issues of desire, rage, power, and need, on the other. In the war of words that framed a liberation movement, some kinds of abuse stories gained traction while others remained untold.

In Hard Knocks, rather than interviewing women who used the movement to escape violence, Haaken talked to the people who staffed the movement – volunteers, program directors, political activists. She interviewed more than 200 persons working in the field to discern how their interventions may have unconsciously structured victims’ accounts in particular ways that did not necessarily reflect the totality of the women's experiences so much as reify a particular dimension that might be useful in the fight to have domestic violence treated seriously by legislators, police, the judiciary, and the public. She also investigated the scripting of psychological narratives that ignore cultural context, and media portrayals that theatricalize human suffering.

Haaken understands the usefulness of a feminist narrative for the fledgling movement but recognizes the potential harm of such reductionism. Her book pokes the places where the movement narrative has become particularly ossified and may no longer serve the interests of the women it was designed to help. She examines the classification of domestic violence as a “special case” of violence, tensions between the movement and the State, internecine battles around issues of class and race, and conflicts between a feminist versus psychological analysis of domestic violence. Her subject is the stories each side procures and polishes. Haaken's incisive rhetorical strategy is to defang competing “facts” by positing them instead as the myths and countermyths that constitute popular narratives about battered women.

On a Sunday morning in 2009 near Seattle, Maurice Clemmons, a middle-aged African American man, shot four white policemen. The ensuing media coverage of the manhunt, and numerous legal system failures to contain Clemmons eclipsed any alternative pursuit to uncover and explore the social and environmental forces that may have helped shape Clemmons' psychological structure. In making a scapegoat of Clemmons, Seattle missed the opportunity to explore the long-term and insidious psychological impact of oppression, poverty, racism, and cultural violence. The author also explores individual and community psychological structure within the overarching metaphor and model of plate tectonics.

In this excellent and provocative book, Will Stockton presents a challenge to the tone, structure, method, and periodization of the paradigm-shift-with-case-studies model of historicist scholarship that has prevailed for the last two decades in early modern literary studies. Adopting an authorial voice that is engaging and without contrivance, and reveling in every pun that the subject matter allows, Stockton works through a series of innovative theoretical moves to make psychoanalysis a subtle, nondeterministic mode for the analysis of literary texts and their encompassing cultures.

Five chapters on authors and works, both canonical and obscure, follow a dense introduction that importantly and necessarily establishes the study's psychoanalytic bona fides and validates the use of psychoanalytic models for critical investigation. Stockton begins with an odd reading of a famous moment in Hamlet, the hero's unkempt appearance to Ophelia, including “stockings fouled,” which “testifies readily enough to the fact that Hamlet has been traumatized by his encounter with his father's ghost” (p. ix). But for whose benefit is this testimony? It could be only for someone who knows about the ghost but not about the antic disposition, which is, no one. If the testimony is meant for the play's audience, then we must assume that Hamlet's disheveled appearance is not a deliberate subterfuge and that the antic disposition has broken down into actual madness. Murray Schwartz  

Those friends thou hast, and their adoption tried

Grapple them unto thy soul with hoops of steel.

Shakespeare

With shocking suddenness, Elisabeth Young-Bruehl died on December 1, 2011 at the age of 65. In a sign of our times, within hours, her Wikipedia entry recorded the event with brutal finality, even as the news echoed through the networks of relatives, friends, colleagues and students. “Pulmonary embolism, returning from a concert.” A vibrant and rich life seemed transformed in no time into a stream of personal and public tributes. The summing up began, and it continues, but a sense of unreality attends her stunning and abrupt loss. Words pour into the void.

Elisabeth died in medias res (she would have liked the Latin phrase), as she was preparing to celebrate the publication of her latest book, Childism: Confronting Prejudice Against Children (Yale University Press, 2011). During the previous months the entries in her blog, “Who's Afraid of Social Democracy?” had been arriving on the internet with characteristic regularity, and she was immersed in her latest massive project, a multivolume, definitive edition of the works of D.W. Winnicott. Also yet to come was a book about dreams that symbolize the self and its development, to which she had alluded periodically; and, no doubt, we could have expected the regular gifts of essays and reviews. Her disciplined production of important work was astonishing. Where others would be depleted by the labor of writing, she was like the Biblical burning bush, energized by her own creativity and calling. Her work fills a shelf in my study.

military sexual trauma; military sexual assault; incest narratives; military diagnosis; psychology and military; gender and military culture

As part of preproduction research for a documentary film on mental health practices in the United States military, this field note takes up findings related to discursive strategies deployed by the US Department of Defense and Veterans Administration programs in preventing and treating military sexual trauma. In the analysis of dozens of training manuals and interviews with therapists working in Sexual Assault Prevention teams through the Army National Guard and the VA, the analogy of military sexual assault and incest emerged as a recurring motif. The authors pursue the question of whether the analogy is progressive or regressive from the perspective of women service members. The authors situate their arguments in a line of analysis pursued in the earlier work of Haaken that explains how real accounts of abuse acquire social symbolic loadings over time in ways that are open to both conservative and progressive interpretations.

the dreaming, Dadirri, trauma, catastrophe, aboriginal culture, community

The Dreaming and Dadirri were cultural phenomena of early Australian Aboriginals. From them we gain ideas of how trauma was treated and the roots of how we treat trauma today. This paper attempts to give understanding of the catastrophe that befell the Aboriginal peoples resulting from dislocation from culture and loss of continuity through stolen children, community and land. The tragedy that has ensued leaves these people devoid of protection from within their own psyche and the current world they live in. Can psychoanalytic therapy, with its focus on the symbolic, with its use of the ancient form of The Dreaming and Dadirri help restore their internal world?

Holocaust, genocide, attachment, body, soma, Haydée Faimberg

Haydée Faimberg's case of Mario is investigated through the lens of Kleinian and relational theory as well as trauma studies. We revisit Mario's bodily communications in the analysis, when he is narrating money and history. Massive trauma ruptures human bonds. In my view, Mario's madness is restorative of these human bonds. drive, fantasy, Oedipus, becoming, Deleuze and Guattari

The publication of Deleuze and Guattari's Anti-Oedipus proclaimed the demise of Oedipus and initiated a harsh critique of Freudian psychoanalysis. Ever since, Deleuze and Guatarri have been read mainly in opposition to Lacan and Freud. Using the science fiction film Minority Report as an example this paper attempts to balance the two approaches. It focuses on two themes emerging from the film: the experience of ‘becoming’ alongside the question a contemporary Oedipus might ask instead of ‘Who am I?’, and the relationship between individuals and society in the light of the ‘better world’ that is emerging as a collective contemporary ideal.

This paper considers Winnicott's notion of maturity as distinct from the themes of consolation and renunciation in the Freudian interpretation of culture. trauma, resilience, Lacan, marginalization, psychosocial origins of psychosis

Psychological resilience is built on the capacity accurately to reflect on one's thoughts and feelings in relation to the thoughts and feelings of others. The strong link between bullying and psychosis highlights ways in which social isolation inhibits the development of these capacities. Prevailing ideas about psychosis tend further to marginalize individuals already struggling with social isolation. We present interview data that show ways in which identified patients may stumble over diagnoses, thereby exacerbating extant cognitive or perceptual difficulties. In striking contrast, a Lacanian perspective marks the importance of recognizing the Subject in the context of experienced difficulties. Such a view is supported by outcome data that highlight the importance of attending to the psychosocial contexts in which psychosis arises, and the human connections through which such distress might be moderated.

Valerie Walkerdine

Valerie Walkerdine  

psychosocial methods, male unemployment, masculinities, emotions, labour market change

Using a psychosocial approach, this paper explores young unemployed men's resistance to work they describe as ‘embarrassing’ and ‘feminine’. The context is the closure of a steelworks in a town in the South Wales valleys, in which their resistance is mediated by father–son relationships that dictate what counts as proper manly work. In this study, young men, as well as their mothers and (where possible) their fathers, were interviewed. The interviews reveal a community suffering the effects of intergenerational trauma and riven with complex feelings about masculinity and femininity. These feelings are projected onto the young men, who feel bullied and shamed by their families, peers and others in the community because they are unable to find gender-appropriate work. The implications of these findings for understandings of youth male unemployment are considered.

This article suggests that the arguably arcane setting of the consultation room provides a unique space in which questions about online engagement can be explored. The contemporary state of affairs with regard to social networking and Google is examined in relation to a clinical example that serves as a reference point from which to open broader questions about our culture's relationship to the internet. A relational psychoanalytic approach is utilised to theorise online relations with reference to the ‘analytic third’ and the developing concept of ‘virtual impingement’.

Anti-Semitism in Germany, defense of guilt and shame, intergenerational transmission, qualitative method, group discussion, interviews

Anti-Semitism is a worldwide phenomenon whose continuity in Germany cannot be understood without analyzing the aftermaths of Nazi Germany and the Holocaust. This is one of the central findings of a qualitative and psychoanalytically oriented study of the psychical aftermaths in non-Jewish Germans as a result of the National Socialist extermination of the Jews. The background of the research project was the 1941 deportation of Jews from a German city to the ghetto of Minsk (Belarus), where about 135,000 Jews were murdered between 1941 and 1943. In a group discussion, non-Jewish Germans who had witnessed this deportation as schoolboys in 1941 were asked to speak about their memories of the deportation. This discussion was followed by interviews with most of the participants and some of their children. The interpretation of the qualitative material is discussed in relation to psychoanalytic concepts on the defenses of guilt and shame and their intergenerational transmission.

Miyazaki, animated films, Japan, childhood, emotional development

This article explores the Japanese animated films of Hayao Miyazaki and Studio Ghibli, which are outstanding contributions to contemporary popular culture. It describes their representation of developmental experiences of children and adolescents and compares them with work in the British and American traditions of children's fiction. It deploys psychoanalytic perspectives to suggest that one of their many admirable qualities is their sensitivity to the unconscious anxieties of normal children. While the films belong broadly in the genre of fantasy, they nevertheless convey a subtle awareness of social differences and changes. Their traditional method of hand-drawn animation is shown to make possible a great diversity and delicacy of visual representation. The films provide many beautiful animated representations of natural, man-made, and imagined environments and express deep concerns. After an overview of Miyazaki's work, the article gives a more detailed consideration of Our Neighbour Totoro, Ponyo, and Porco Rosso.

qualitative research, ecology, environment, melancholia, climate, sustainability

This essay presents a narrative of a psychosocial research investigation into the complex experiences of environmental degradation, conducted as a field study in Green Bay, Wisconsin. Using in-depth, psychoanalytically informed research interviews, the study explored the presence of ambivalent, contradictory narratives, suggesting that the experience of environmental degradation may in fact be constituted in part by loss and mourning, which may manifest as a form of environmental melancholia. Such insights are directly relevant for how we conceptualize and imagine theories of agency, engagement and participation. I discuss aspects of the research design, methodology, opportunities and challenges of the project and suggest the need to apply qualitative, psychosocial research methods to the immensely challenging and charged ecological challenges we currently face.

Sara Wasson Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010, 224pp, cloth, $84.00, ISBN 978-0-230-57753-4

‘There are problems’, states Sara Wasson, ‘with using psychoanalysis or its derivatives to explain Gothic, not least the fact that psychoanalysis is arguably itself a Gothic fiction, albeit a hundred years late to the party’ (pp. 25–26). Then, employing a critical gaze through a range of wartime literary texts, she carefully sets out her strategy for deploying aspects of psychoanalytic theory embedded in attention to the sociohistorical context of World War II as experienced in London. Wasson is an adept writer who implements psychoanalytic tropes well to lay bare the uncanny at the core of wartime writers and artists. These authors knowingly created a cognitive dissonance in their texts to capture the familiar-yet-strange that was present in wartime London – a sense of subversive otherness that was not tamed by dominant redemptive stories of national triumph or stoic Blitz unity. Wasson shows that, as always, there are strangers and dark secrets hidden in the shadows of London's streets, domestic spaces, hospitals, morgues, factories, internment camps and psychiatric hospitals. An inhospitable, unhomely Gothic-like homeland for some …

Critical analysts of the Gothic have regularly turned to psychoanalytical models in recent years; the theories of fragmentation, repression, ambivalent desire and disgust that Freud and his successors interrogated so provocatively have cast new light on the shadowy world of Gothic fiction. As established analysts of Gothic literature have long observed, from its eighteenth-century manifestations through to the late twentieth-century revivals of Gothic fiction through postmodernism, the Gothic tropes of alienation, confinement, decay and corruption mark and disturb the easy closure of modernity's grand narratives.

Stand-up comedy binds dramatic cultural spectacle to ritualised, intimate exposure. Examining ‘case’ examples from live comic performance, this paper describes stand-up as a kind of social dreaming. The article proposes a theoretical frame drawing on Thomas Ogden's notion of ‘talking as dreaming’ and psychoanalytic accounts connecting humour and melancholia. Locating the stand-up comedian's propensity for humour in a specialist capacity to hone, display and process traumata, the paper characterises stand-up as a performative oscillation evoking paranoid-schizoid and depressive anxieties. The primary aim of this article is to clarify Lacan’s understanding of the graph of desire through a close reading of Seminar V, in which a double debate with Klein and Marx is engaged. With this clarification, I contest Žižek’s view that identifies the lower level of the graph with the symbolic, and the upper level with the symbolic shot through by the real. According to him, while at the lower level the “alienation” of the subject in the symbolic transpires, at the upper level the “separation” of the subject from the symbolic itself becomes conceivable as the dimension of the real is introduced. Against this construal, I identify the lower level with the imaginary, and the upper level with the symbolic. Žižek’s misapprehension results from neglecting the distinction Lacan makes between the symbolic that arrives in advance in the imaginary phase itself and the symbolic proper. In the concluding section, I attempt to draw out some of the main implications that this clarification has for the Lacanian critique of ideology.

Childhood adversity and psychosis: A literature review with clinical and societal implications

Daniel Skehan , Warren Larkin and John Read

John Read

UK

John Read  

childhood adversity, abuse, psychosis, schizophrenia

There is a substantial body of research indicating an association between childhood adversity and later psychosis. Cross-sectional, correlational studies have given way to large-scale, case-controlled studies which indicate a dose-response association indicative of a causal relationship. Several psychological and biological models have been proposed which offer credible accounts of the processes by which trauma may increase the risk of psychosis, including cognitive, psychodynamic, dissociation and attachment perspectives. Clinically it is imperative routinely to enquire about traumatic experiences, to respond appropriately and to offer psychosocial treatments to those who report traumatic life events in the context of psychotic experiences.

[[RunningHead]]

The subject of psychosis: A Lacanian perspective

Manya Steinkoler

Manya Steinkoler

USA

Manya Steinkoler  

Stijn Vanheule, Palgrave, Macmillan, 2011, 208pp., $80.00, $50.00, ISBN-10: 978-0230276644; ISBN-13: 978-0230276642

Stijn Vanheule's well written and scholarly, The Subject of Psychosis: A Lacanian Perspective, could not be more timely for clinicians, researchers, scholars in psychoanalysis, and even for the educated layperson interested in understanding psychosis from a Lacanian perspective. In what Lipovetsky has called our “hypermodern times,” when reality is increasingly virtual and we are asked to respond more and more to imaginary demands to consume and enjoy, thinking about psychosis clinically is indispensable. An important contribution to Lacanian work in English, Vanheule's text is a much-needed, theoretically clear, lucid, sophisticated and critical understanding of Lacanian theory on psychosis. Vanheule breaks down Lacan's work on psychosis into four distinct periods: “The age of imaginary identification/The Mirror Stage” (1930s–1950), “The age of the primacy of the signifier/The Name of the Father” (1950 s), “The age of the object a” (1960 s), and “The age of the knot/Jouissance and the Real” (1970 s).

It is important to remark on the title of Vanheule's text: Lacanians have maintained that there is no subject in psychosis since the subject is an effect of the signifier, i.e., the subject is a symbolic effect. Vanheule's title allows us to consider the subject of psychosis in a variety of ways: as the Real of psychotic suffering, as a topic of study, and as related to the clinical subject who works with psychotics.

Through all of the chapters, by way of Lacan's changing theorizations and re-conceptualizations, Vanheule provides a broad and variegated understanding of psychosis. He explains the three Lacanian registers and how they operate in psychosis. The Real, the register of jouissance, is fundamental to the psychotic who is plagued with jouissance at the level of the body. The Symbolic, which concerns language and representation, is deficient for the psychotic subject, and the Imaginary, which concerns the ego and the image of the body, is also potentially deficient and presents differently in paranoia and schizophrenia. The Real and the Imaginary are the primary registers for psychosis and insofar as the Symbolic is deficient, language remains imaginarized for the psychotic subject. Vanheule explains that the body of the psychotic subject is a “Real” body, not drained of jouissance by language or moored by the mirror. This is due to the fact that the object has not become separated, allowing for the birth of a subject (as it has with neurotics), but rather remains fused with the subject. (The objet a covers up the Real of Being for neurotics, who locate the object in the other.) Jouissance is thus not localized but threatens constantly to invade, often finding stability only in the delusional metaphor.
